title: Two Squares That Sum to C
statement:
You get a non-negative integer c. Return true if there are two whole numbers a ≥ 0 and b ≥ 0 with a² + b² = c.

a and b may be equal, and either may be 0.

examples.why: The squares up to 3 are 0 and 1, and no two of them add up to 3.
4 + 4. The same square can be used twice, so a search that demands a < b misses it.

hints: a can only range from 0 to √c. For each a, what must b² be?
Checking whether c − a² is a perfect square takes O(1) with an integer square root, giving O(√c) total.
Or use two pointers: a = 0, b = ⌊√c⌋. If a² + b² is too small, raise a; if too big, lower b.

explain.intuition:
Both numbers are at most √c, so the search space is a √c by √c grid. Put a at the bottom (0) and b at the top (⌊√c⌋). If the sum is too big, no larger a can help this b, so b is useless and you lower it. If the sum is too small, no smaller b can help this a, so you raise a. Each step throws away a whole row or column of the grid.

It is the same idea as finding a pair with a target sum in a sorted list; here the sorted list is the squares 0, 1, 4, 9, … and it is never written out.
steps: If s === c, return true. If s < c, increase a. Otherwise decrease b.
pitfalls: Using a < b as the loop condition. Then 8 = 2² + 2² is missed.
Trusting a floating point square root for large c without correcting it. Compare r * r against the target after rounding.
In languages with 32-bit ints, a² + b² can overflow near 2³¹. Use a 64-bit type.

solutions.title: Check the remainder for each a
solutions.idea: For each a from 0 to √c, test whether c − a² is a perfect square.

solutions.title: Two pointers over the squares
solutions.idea: Start with the smallest and largest candidates and move whichever side cannot be part of an answer.

followups: Return every pair (a, b) with a ≤ b. How many can there be?
Number theory says c works exactly when every prime of the form 4k + 3 appears to an even power. Use that for an O(√c) factoring solution — is it faster in practice?
